narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants to admit students likely to pass, this probability led to the rejection of your application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were, in order: your first-year grades in law school, your LSAT score, and your third-year grades. Your first-year performance was the strongest reason the model leaned toward failure. Being in the fourth decile is noticeably lower than the average of sixth decile among students who were accepted, and this gap pushed the prediction strongly toward not passing the bar. Your LSAT score of 35 also worked against you; it sits below the 37.2 average of accepted students and added further weight toward a failure prediction. Your third-year grades, by contrast, worked mildly in your favor. A fifth-decile ranking is only slightly below the 5.8 average of accepted students, so this gave a small nudge in the direction of passing.

Taken together, the model saw your early academic record and test score as clear signals that the risk of failing the bar was too high for admission. 

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your first-year performance and consider retaking the LSAT if possible. Improving those two areas would have the biggest impact on future predictions and on your actual likelihood of passing the bar.
